readings.title: A library card for evening learners
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
An adult college and a library wanted evening students to borrow books after class. The existing registration desk closed before most lessons ended. The main obstacle was registration hours that excluded late learners. Students could browse shelves but could not complete identity checks or take books home during their first visit. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used a short late-desk trial. Staff opened the counter after two classes each week and recorded how many students needed help with new cards. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated most requests came immediately after class. Learners valued speaking to a person, but few arrived during other extended hours. The group then introduced a focused half-hour service window. The library matched staffing to class endings and published clear instructions for students arriving on different evenings. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: service hours should follow real learning routines. A small change at the right time mattered more than opening the entire building late every night. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in a library card for evening learners, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records.

readings.title: Choosing books for a shared shelf
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A community centre offered a shelf where adults could exchange books. Donations arrived quickly, but many volumes stayed untouched. The main obstacle was a collection that did not match local interests. Several shelves held old reference books while visitors asked for short novels and practical guides. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used a month of borrowing notes and requests. Volunteers recorded which books moved and invited suggestions without asking people to reveal personal reading histories. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated short practical titles circulated most often. The records challenged an early assumption that larger academic books would be the main attraction. The group then introduced a smaller shelf with rotating categories. The centre passed unwanted donations to suitable organisations and made room for the kinds of books residents requested. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: a useful collection responds to its readers. The number of donated books was less important than whether people could find something they wanted to use. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in choosing books for a shared shelf, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Computer lessons at different starting points
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A library offered a single introductory computer course. Some learners had never used a mouse, while others only needed help with forms. The main obstacle was one lesson pace for widely different skills. Beginners felt rushed and experienced participants waited through material they already understood. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used a short task-based starting session. Tutors asked learners to try a few everyday tasks and describe which ones they hoped to master. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated goals differed more than ages did. People of similar ages showed very different experience, so age was a poor guide for grouping them. The group then introduced two learning paths with optional support. The library offered basic device practice and a separate practical forms session, with the option to move between them. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: adult learning should begin with actual needs. A respectful starting point helps learners progress without assuming what they already know. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in computer lessons at different starting points, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A quieter corner for study
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A busy library planned to add study seats. Staff first counted empty chairs, but students complained about interruptions rather than capacity. The main obstacle was noise spilling into a study area. The nearby help desk attracted conversations, and a sign asking for silence could not change the desk’s purpose. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used observation of movement and sound. Staff watched where groups gathered and invited readers to describe when they needed a quiet place. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated one corner stayed calm during peak hours. It was farther from the entrance but close to good lighting and accessible routes. The group then introduced study tables moved to the calm corner. The help desk remained where visitors could find it, while clear signs identified the new quiet area. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: a seat is useful only in the right setting. Counting furniture alone could not reveal why some places supported concentrated reading. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in a quieter corner for study, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
Projects concerning libraries and lifelong learning often begin with a practical question. People may agree on a general goal while experiencing the same service in different ways. In this case, local organizers invited residents to describe ordinary visits and kept simple records of what happened. They compared those accounts before changing the neighbourhood library programme. The first trial did not answer every question, but it showed which difficulties were repeated and which were temporary. Staff then explained the reasons for a modest adjustment. Clear information helped people understand the decision, including those who would have preferred another option. The group planned to review the arrangement again after more people had used it.

translation.referenceAnswer: 有关图书馆与终身学习的项目通常从一个实际问题开始。人们可能赞同总体目标，却对同一服务有不同体验。在这个案例中，当地组织者请居民描述日常使用情况，并简单记录发生的事情。他们对照这些叙述后调整了服务。最初的试行无法回答所有问题，但能显示哪些困难反复出现，哪些只是暂时现象。工作人员随后解释了一项适度调整的原因。清楚的信息帮助人们理解决定，包括那些更希望采用其他方案的人。团队计划在更多人使用后再次评估安排。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the library team proposing a small improvement to the neighbourhood library programme. Explain the problem, describe a short trial, and say what evidence should guide the final decision.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the neighbourhood library programme. People have noticed registration hours that excluded late learners, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
